name: PostgreSQL performance improvements
description:
PostgreSQL performance improvements

Aims

  • To provide configuration parameters that may be tuned to improve performance.
  • To provide details on identifying and examining queries with poor performance.

Assumptions

  • PostgreSQL is installed and running
  • A sample database is installed
  • User has root access to the server AND to postgres
  • User has basic familiarity with Linux

Contents

  1. Tuning PostgreSQL program parameters
  2. Using 'IDENTIFY' and 'EXAMINE' to locate poor performance

name: Tuning PostgreSQL
description:
1. Tuning PostgreSQL program parameters

Some postgres program parameters may help improve performance in some areas. For example if you are working with very large datasets, you can change the amount of memory allocated to postgres to improve performance.

NOTE Any changes you make here will affect the rest of the Linux system as well. If there are other important services running on the same server you may first want to migrate your database to a dedicated server instead.

NOTE Tweaking the program parameters may only display performance improvements on larger datasets, or under high-load situations. You will need to simulate these conditions in order to see whether the changes have had any effect.

NOTE The parameters you tweak and the values you choose are HIGHLY dependant on your physical server properties (Memory, CPU, HDD size, HDD speed).

NOTE BACK UP your configuration file before you change it. Even better, store it in a version control system like CVS or Git.

By default the postgresql configuration file is stored in /var/lib/pgsql/9.4/data/postgresql.conf

1.1 Increase 'shared_buffers'

The default value is 

shared_buffers = 128MB                  # min 128kB

Change this to between 5% and 15% of total system memory

The number you choose depends on what other processes are running on the same machine.

On a DEDICATED machine, which only runs PostgreSQL, you can set this value to 15%

On a SHARED machine, you should set this to a lower value.

Dedicated machine with 8GB RAM:

shared_buffers = 1024MB            # 15% of available RAM

Shared machine with many other services and 8GB RAM:

shared_buffers = 400MB            # 5% of available RAM

RESTART PostgreSQL after changing this parameter.

1.2 Increase 'effective_cache_size'

This setting controls how much space will be used for caching table data.

By default this setting is commented out.

On DEDICATED machines, you can set this up to 25% of your "available RAM"

To check your "available RAM" start up all normal services on your Linux machine and run the following command:

[root@centos ~]# free -m
         total       used       free     shared    buffers     cached
Mem:          7967       2117       5849         21         80       1142
-/+ buffers/cache:        894       7072
Swap:         1023          0       1023

Look at the 'free' column. Here it shows that '5849Mb' of RAM is available for use.

Therefore on a DEDICATED machine, you can use up to (5849/4=) 1462Mb of RAM for cacheing.

Change the setting in the postgresql.conf file:

#effective_cache_size = 4GB

to

effective_cache_size = 1462Mb

1.3 Increase 'work_mem'

This parameter controls how much memory will be used when running 'SORT' on queries.

This can improve performance if you have a lot of SQL queries which include an 'ORDER BY' or 'DISTINCT' clause, or a merge 'JOIN'.

Note This parameter affects every single sort individually. So if you have 30 users all running queries, and you set this parameter to 50Mb, you will use 30*50=1500MB of RAM.

By default this setting is commented out.

Change the setting in the postgresql.conf file:

#work_mem = 4MB                         # min 64kB

to

work_mem = 8MB                         # min 64kB

1.4 Reduce 'random_page_cost'

This parameter gives an estimation of the "cost" of accessing non-sequential data, in other words data which is randomly spread out. If you have fast SSD disks or SCSI RAID arrays, you can reduce this parameter slightly as the cost of reading from disk will be lower.

You should set this value to a multiple of the 'seq_page_cost' variable, and uncomment both

Change the settings in the postgresql.conf file:

#seq_page_cost = 1.0                    # measured on an arbitrary scale
#random_page_cost = 4.0                 # same scale as above

to

seq_page_cost = 1.0                    # measured on an arbitrary scale
random_page_cost = 3.0                 # same scale as above

1.5 Ensure 'track_counts' and 'autovacuum' are both enabled and set to ON

'Vacuuming' means cleaning out old (deleted or updated) data in database tables. Each time you DELETE or UPDATE a row, the original values will be marked as 'dead' in the table, but will not be deleted.

You can run vacuums manually but it is better to allow the system to run them automatically as required. This involves enabling two settings:

Change the settings in the postgresql.conf file:

#track_counts = on

#autovacuum = on                        # Enable autovacuum subprocess?  'on'

to

track_counts = on

autovacuum = on                        # Enable autovacuum subprocess?  'on'

1.6 Restart PostgreSQL to apply all the changes.

Make sure that all your changes are picked up by restarting PostgreSQL:

[root@centos tmp]# service postgresql-9.4 restart

name: IDENTIFY and EXAMINE
description:
2. Using 'IDENTIFY' and 'EXAMINE' to locate poor performance

The 'EXPLAIN' command shows the execution plan of a SQL statement.

If you have a SQL statement such as

SELECT * from work where workid='tempest';

you can prefix it with 'EXPLAIN' to show the system's estimated cost of running the query, and the method it will take to resolve the query:

shakespeare=# explain select * from work where workid='tempest';
 Seq Scan on work  (cost=0.00..1.54 rows=1 width=412)
   Filter: ((workid)::text = 'tempest'::text)

shakespeare=#

This shows the system will perform a SEQUENTIAL SCAN on the table 'work', which it estimates will cost between 0.00 and 1.54 (arbitrary values).

To see the actual time taken to run the query, add the command 'ANALYZE':

shakespeare=# explain analyze select * from work where workid='tempest';
 Seq Scan on work  (cost=0.00..1.54 rows=1 width=412) (actual time=0.026..0.029 rows=1 loops=1)
   Filter: ((workid)::text = 'tempest'::text)
   Rows Removed by Filter: 42
 Planning time: 0.109 ms
 Execution time: 0.060 ms

shakespeare=#

Here you see that execution of the query completed in 0.060 ms.

On more complicated queries, and nested queries, you will see diffent data:

shakespeare=# explain analyze select longtitle from work where workid in (select workid from paragraph where plainText like '%pierces%');
 Nested Loop Semi Join  (cost=0.00..2186.68 rows=3 width=146) (actual time=35.193..35.283 rows=2 loops=1)
   Join Filter: ((work.workid)::text = (paragraph.workid)::text)
   Rows Removed by Join Filter: 83
   ->  Seq Scan on work  (cost=0.00..1.43 rows=43 width=228) (actual time=0.012..0.047 rows=43 loops=1)
   ->  Materialize  (cost=0.00..2183.33 rows=3 width=9) (actual time=0.591..0.816 rows=2 loops=43)
     ->  Seq Scan on paragraph  (cost=0.00..2183.31 rows=3 width=9) (actual time=25.350..34.970 rows=2 loops=1)
           Filter: (plaintext ~~ '%pierces%'::text)
           Rows Removed by Filter: 35463
 Planning time: 0.503 ms
 Execution time: 35.354 ms

shakespeare=#

Here you see the query required the following steps:

  • Sequential Scan on paragraph
  • Sequential Scan on work
  • Join filter on workid

The query took 35.354ms to run.

With EXPLAIN and ANALYZE you can get an immediate indication of how long your SQL statements are taking to complete.

This can alert you to queries which are taking a long time to complete.

Also be aware that some queries may run relatively quickly, but are run very often. Optimising a common query can often give better results than optimising a query which is seldom used.

Note Details returned by EXPLAIN and ANALYZE do not take in to account network transmission costs, so if you are sending a large amount of data across the network this may slow down your query even more.

Note Running EXPLAIN and ANALYZE has an overhead. Therefore the results you get from the commands only give you an idea of the 'relative' performance of the query, not the 'absolute' performance.

By using these commands, you can identify queries that could be optimised by the development team.
